18	
19	# 论文写作风格规范
20	
21	> 核心哲学：**论文是一个有说服力的故事，不是实验报告。** 审稿人在几十秒内判断论文价值——如果 Abstract 和 Introduction 读起来像实验日志，论文就已经失败了。
22	
23	---
24	
25	## 一、总体写作哲学
26	
27	### 1.1 故事驱动，不是数据堆砌
28	
29	- 论文必须以"故事线"为核心展开：问题 → 洞察 → 方法 → 验证
30	- 禁止大量实验数据堆砌——每个数字出现必须服务于叙事推进
31	- 附录内容必须在正文中有明确引用且融入叙事，禁止简单堆砌
32	- 如果附录数据对核心叙事有重大影响，根据附录数据调整论文 framing
33	
34	### 1.2 主线统一性
35	
36	- 当 idea 在研究过程中发生变化后，**必须重审全文逻辑**
37	- 常见问题：Introduction 讲的故事 A，Method 做的是故事 B，Results 又在讲故事 C
38	- 修复方式：从最终实验结论反推，重写 Introduction 的问题定义和动机
39	- 每次 idea 调整后检查：Abstract → Introduction → Method → Results → Discussion → Conclusion 是否形成一条连贯主线
40	
41	### 1.3 专有名词必须有定义
42	
43	- 首次出现的专有名词/缩写必须给出完整定义和解释
44	- Abstract 中使用的缩写也必须在 Abstract 内定义（如 LLM = Large Language Model）
45	- 不能假设读者知道你自己定义的术语——论文从来没解释过的概念不能直接使用
46	- 通用规则：如果一个非标准术语第一次出现时没有括号定义，就是写作 bug
47	
48	### 1.4 写作前必读同类优秀论文
49	
50	- 每个章节动笔前，找 **2-3 篇目标会议近 1-2 年的高分论文**作为风格参考——同类问题或同类方法皆可
51	- 重点学：
52	  - Abstract 怎么用最少篇幅讲完故事
53	  - Introduction 怎么从大问题切入到具体贡献
54	  - Related Work 怎么 positioning 自己（不是 survey）
55	  - Table/Figure 怎么压缩信息密度
56	- **不是抄袭**，是学习同行的故事节奏和审美——不同子领域叙事节奏差异很大
57	- 实操：Paper Agent 可以从 `literature_map.yaml` 中挑 `role=foundation` 或 `role=direct-competitor` 的论文，把 `{title, venue, year, abstract}` 附在 Worker 的 task_prompt 中作为概念参考；如需学习写作风格本身，让 Worker 通过 WebSearch 取得论文链接并 fetch 全文
58	
59	---
60	
61	## 二、Abstract 写作规范
62	
63	### 2.1 四个必答问题（150-250 words）
64	
65	Abstract 必须在很短的篇幅内清楚回答：
66	1. **研究什么问题** — 1-2 句话交代背景和痛点
67	2. **为什么重要** — 现有方法的不足（不用写太多）
68	3. **本文提出什么** — 核心贡献的关键机制（简要，不堆砌细节）
69	4. **结果说明什么** — 用具体实验结论支撑贡献
70	
71	### 2.2 禁忌
72	
73	- **禁止堆砌数据**：Abstract 不是 Results 的缩写。最多引用 2-3 个关键数字，要服务于 claim
74	- **

17	# LaTeX 论文写作全流程
18	
19	ML/AI 顶会论文从草稿到投稿的完整指南。整合 Orchestra Research、VibeSkills、claim2evidence 三方最佳实践。
20	
21	---
22	
23	## 1. 工作模式
24	
25	开始前选择模式：
26	
27	| 模式 | 说明 | 适用 |
28	|------|------|------|
29	| **Build** | 从实验笔记/结果/代码生成论文 | 新稿 |
30	| **Improve** | 改写已有章节，强化论证 | 修改稿 |
31	| **Audit** | 输出风险列表 + 缺失证据 + 修复建议 | 投前检查 |
32	
33	---
34	
35	## 2. Claim-Evidence 方法论
36	
37	**核心原则：论文是一个有中心贡献的故事，不是实验的堆砌。**
38	
39	### 2.1 一句话贡献
40	
41	在写任何内容之前，必须能用一句话说清贡献。如果不能，说明还没准备好写论文。
42	
43	### 2.2 Claim-Evidence Map
44	
45	为每个 contribution 建立 claim→evidence 映射表：
46	
47	| Contribution | Claim | Evidence | Table/Figure |
48	|-------------|-------|----------|-------------|
49	| C1: 方法 X 在 Y 上 SOTA | 比所有 baseline 高 ≥2% | 5-seed 平均，p<0.05 | Table 1 |
50	| C2: 消融证明 Z 是关键 | 去掉 Z 后掉 >5% | 消融实验 | Table 2 |
51	| C3: 计算效率 | 比 baseline 快 3× | FLOPs + wall-clock | Figure 3 |
52	
53	**没有直接证据支撑的 claim 必须删除或降级为 discussion。**
54	
55	### 2.3 章节起草顺序
56	
57	```
58	1. Introduction + Experiments（先确定 claim 和 evidence）
59	2. Method（评估问题稳定后再写细节）
60	3. Related Work
61	4. Abstract + Title（核心 claim 定型后最后写）
62	```
63	
64	### 2.4 Quality Gates
65	
66	投稿前必须通过：
67	- [ ] 前两段出现显式 novelty 声明
68	- [ ] 每个 contribution 有可验证的 evidence
69	- [ ] Abstract / Intro / Conclusion 的 claim 一致
70	- [ ] Limitations 真实且技术性诚实
71	- [ ] 审稿人两分钟内能识别 delta
72	
73	---
74	
75	## 3. 引用防幻觉（CRITICAL）
76	
77	**AI 生成引用有 ~40% 错误率。绝对禁止凭记忆写 BibTeX。**
78	
79	### 3.1 黄金法则
80	
81	```
82	IF 无法程序化获取引用:
83	    → 标记 [CITATION NEEDED] 或 \cite{PLACEHOLDER_verify}
84	    → 明确告知用户
85	    → 绝不编造看似合理的引用
86	```
87	
88	### 3.2 五步验证流程
89	
90	```
91	1. SEARCH  → Semantic Scholar API 搜索关键词
92	2. VERIFY  → 至少 2 个来源确认论文存在（S2 + arXiv/CrossRef）
93	3. RETRIEVE → 通过 DOI 获取 BibTeX（程序化，非记忆）
94	4. CHECK   → 确认

2	\label{sec:experimental_setup}
3	
4	\subsection{Architectures and Benchmark}
5	\label{sec:setup_overview}
6	
7	We study five VLA architectures spanning three vision connector families (Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}).
8	
9	\textbf{Linear projection.} $\pi_0$~\cite{black2024pi0} (3.3B parameters, 256 tokens) maps SigLIP~\cite{zhai2023siglip} patches through a linear layer into a PaliGemma backbone and generates actions via flow matching~\cite{lipman2023flow}. X-VLA~\cite{zheng2025xvla} (880M parameters, 50 tokens) augments its linear projection with a 12-layer BART encoder~\cite{lewis2020bart}; self-attention in these layers introduces cross-token mixing that makes the effective pipeline more complex than the nominal ``linear projection'' label suggests.
10	
11	\textbf{MLP projector.} OpenVLA~\cite{kim2024openvla} (7B parameters, 256 tokens) fuses DINOv2~\cite{oquab2023dinov2} and SigLIP encoders through a three-layer MLP (GELU activations) that maps each patch independently into a Llama-2 backbone. OFT~\cite{kim2025openoft} shares this architecture with an optimized fine-tuning action head; we include it for attention entropy comparison only.
12	
13	\textbf{Spatial folding.} SmolVLA~\cite{shukor2025smolvla} (450M parameters, 128 tokens from two cameras) encodes each camera image with SigLIP into 1024 patches, then applies a pixel-shuffle connector that folds each $4{\times}4$ block into one token by channel concatenation (64 per camera). Each token encodes 16 spatially contiguous patches; removing one eliminates an entire $4{\times}4$ receptive field. The tokens enter a Qwen2-0.5B backbone~\cite{yang2024qwen2} with flow matching action generation.

4	We evaluate token pruning across six VLA models spanning three connector families on LIBERO-Object~\cite{liu2023libero} (10 tasks, 50 episodes each, 500 total). All success rates report Wilson 95\% confidence intervals for single-seed results and mean $\pm$ standard deviation for multi-seed results.

6	\subsection{Taxonomy Overview}
7	\label{sec:taxonomy_overview}
8	
9	Table~\ref{tab:taxonomy} organizes seven models into four response classes. The taxonomy reveals that effective vision-to-LLM pipeline complexity, not the nominal connector label or model scale, determines pruning tolerance. Token importance CV tracks this ordering continuously across an 8$\times$ parameter range (450M to 7B): uniformly critical models cluster at CV $< 0.06$, threshold-graded at $\sim$0.15, smooth graded at $\sim$0.22, and catastrophic cliff at $>$0.3. A controlled comparison between $\pi_0$ and OpenVLA (both using 256 SigLIP~\cite{zhai2023siglip} tokens, differing only in connector) yields a 63\,pp gap at $k{=}0.1$, isolating the pipeline as causal (Section~\ref{sec:linear_results}).
10	
11	The four classes differ qualitatively in their failure mode. Uniformly critical models ($\pi_0$, $\pi_0.5$~\cite{black2025pi05}) distribute importance so evenly that no scoring method can identify dispensable tokens; pruning either preserves random spatial coverage (and survives) or removes a clustered patch (and fails). Threshold-graded models (X-VLA) tolerate removal up to a sharp onset point. Smooth graded models (OpenVLA, OFT, CogACT) degrade proportionally to the fraction removed. tool_args.old_string:
Two complementary pruning methods bracket each model's robustness from above and below.

\textbf{L2 norm-based removal} (importance scoring) ranks vision tokens by their L2 norm and physically removes the lowest-norm fraction. Norm ranking preserves the most informative tokens by construction, so L2 removal provides a more favorable test of pruning tolerance.

\textbf{Random removal} (uniform selection) selects tokens uniformly at random and physically removes the unselected ones. Random removal provides a conservative lower bound because it makes no attempt to preserve high-importance tokens.

Model-specific retention ratios reflect each architecture's token count and expected sensitivity. $\pi_0$ is evaluated offline only ($k{=}0.1$, normalized L1 action loss) because its deployment environment precludes closed-loop testing. $\pi_0.5$ uses $k \in \{0.3, 0.5, 0.7\}$ under both L2 and random removal in closed-loop evaluation. X-VLA spans $k \in \{0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.8, 0.85, 0.9, 0.95\}$ with L2 removal across three seeds, providing the finest-grained retention sweep in our study. OpenVLA uses $k \in \{0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 0.95\}$ with random removal as the primary protocol and L2 for direct comparison. SmolVLA tests seven configurations varying scoring (learned ACIS vs.\ random), retention ratio ($k \in \{0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 0.95\}$), and mechanism (zero-masking, true removal, token merging via ToMe~\cite{bolya2023tome}).

The $\pi_0$--OpenVLA pair forms a controlled natural experiment: both consume 256 SigLIP tokens from the same encoder lineage, differing only in their connector (linear projection vs.\ three-layer MLP). Any performance gap at matched retention ratios isolates the connector as the causal factor rather than encoder capacity or token count.
tool_args.new_string:
Two complementary pruning methods bracket each model's robustness from above and below. Both methods physically remove unselected tokens from the sequence (reducing the actual input length to the LLM), rather than zeroing them out; the distinction matters because zero-masking preserves positional structure while physical removal does not.

\textbf{L2 norm-based removal} (importance scoring) ranks vision tokens by their L2 norm and physically removes the lowest-norm fraction. Norm ranking preserves the most informative tokens by construction, so L2 removal provides a more favorable test of pruning tolerance. The underlying assumption is that higher-norm tokens carry more task-relevant information; Section~\ref{sec:scaling_law} examines when this assumption holds and when it fails.

\textbf{Random removal} (uniform selection) selects tokens uniformly at random and physically removes the unselected ones. Random removal provides a conservative lower bound because it makes no attempt to preserve high-importance tokens. For models with near-uniform token norms, however, random selection can outperform L2 by preserving spatial coverage rather than clustering on correlated patches.

Model-specific retention ratios reflect each architecture's token count and expected sensitivity. $\pi_0$ is evaluated offline only ($k{=}0.1$, normalized L1 action loss) because its deployment environment precludes closed-loop testing. $\pi_0.5$ uses $k \in \{0.3, 0.5, 0.7\}$ under both L2 and random removal in closed-loop evaluation, enabling direct method comparison within a single architecture. X-VLA spans $k \in \{0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.8, 0.85, 0.9, 0.95\}$ with L2 removal across three seeds, providing the finest-grained retention sweep in our study and sufficient resolution to locate sharp onset thresholds. OpenVLA uses $k \in \{0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 0.95\}$ with random removal as the primary protocol and L2 for direct comparison. SmolVLA tests seven configurations varying scoring (learned ACIS vs.\ random), retention ratio ($k \in \{0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 0.95\}$), and mechanism (zero-masking, true removal, token merging via ToMe~\cite{bolya2023tome}).

The $\pi_0$--OpenVLA pair forms a controlled natural experiment: both consume 256 SigLIP tokens from the same encoder lineage, differing only in their connector (linear projection vs.\ three-layer MLP). Any performance gap at matched retention ratios isolates the connector as the causal factor rather than encoder capacity or token count. Comparing OpenVLA (random removal, harder test) against X-VLA (L2 removal, easier test) further strengthens architecture-dependent conclusions, because any observed fragility in X-VLA cannot be attributed to an unfavorable scoring method.

tool_args.old_string:
A cross-attention pooling module (22.2M parameters, $\sim$5\% of SmolVLA) is inserted between the pixel-shuffle connector and the LLM backbone. $M$ learned queries attend over all 128 source tokens, producing $M$ compressed representations. The compression sweep covers $M \in \{16, 32, 64, 96, 128\}$, where $M{=}128$ serves as a passthrough control that adds parameters without reducing tokens.

A parameter-matched MLP adapter (22.14M parameters) serves as an architecture control, testing whether the benefit comes from cross-attention specifically or from re-encoding in general. Both VTR and the baseline train from the same SmolVLA-Base checkpoint for 100K steps with identical hyperparameters. An extended training control (same procedure without the compressor) achieves 45.0\% SR, statistically indistinguishable from the 44.8\% baseline ($p > 0.9$); any gain from VTR is therefore architectural, not from additional optimization steps. Training details appear in Appendix~\ref{app:smart_compress_details}.
tool_args.new_string:
A cross-attention pooling module (22.2M parameters, $\sim$5\% of SmolVLA) is inserted between the pixel-shuffle connector and the LLM backbone. $M$ learned queries attend over all 128 source tokens via standard scaled dot-product attention, producing $M$ compressed representations that replace the original 128 tokens as input to the LLM. The compression sweep covers $M \in \{16, 32, 64, 96, 128\}$; $M{=}16$ represents 87.5\% token reduction while $M{=}128$ serves as a passthrough control that adds parameters without reducing tokens.

A parameter-matched MLP adapter (22.14M parameters) serves as an architecture control, testing whether the benefit comes from cross-attention specifically or from re-encoding in general. Both VTR and the baseline train from the same SmolVLA-Base checkpoint for 100K steps with identical hyperparameters. An extended training control (same procedure without the compressor) achieves 45.0\% SR, statistically indistinguishable from the 44.8\% baseline ($p > 0.9$); any gain from VTR is therefore architectural, not from additional optimization steps. VTR results are evaluated with three seeds per configuration to ensure reproducibility. Training details appear in Appendix~\ref{app:smart_compress_details}.

tool_args.old_string: \textbf{Attention entropy ratio} is the normalized Shannon entropy of attention weights over vision tokens. Low entropy indicates concentrated attention on a few tokens, while high entropy reflects diffuse attention across the full token set. CV measures the input-side importance gradient; entropy captures how the downstream LLM allocates attention, providing a complementary view of the same structural property.
tool_args.new_string: \textbf{Attention entropy ratio} is the normalized Shannon entropy of attention weights over vision tokens, computed from the final LLM layer's cross-attention distribution. Low entropy indicates concentrated attention on a few tokens, while high entropy reflects diffuse attention across the full token set. CV measures the input-side importance gradient; entropy captures how the downstream LLM allocates attention, providing a complementary view of the same structural property. OFT and OpenVLA share nearly identical entropy values (0.667 vs.\ 0.661), confirming that the connector, not the action head, determines token utilization patterns. Section~\ref{sec:scaling_law} demonstrates that CV also predicts the optimal pruning strategy: low-CV models require coverage-preserving methods (random selection), while higher-CV models can benefit from importance-based scoring.

Low entropy indicates concentrated attention on a few tokens, while high entropy reflects diffuse attention across the full token set.
